items.subject: Physiology
items.stem: With correct limb-lead placement, which P-wave polarity is expected in normal sinus rhythm?
options: Upright in lead I and inverted in aVR
Upright in lead I and upright in aVR
Inverted in lead I and upright in aVR
Inverted in lead I and inverted in aVR
items.rationale: Normal atrial depolarization travels inferiorly and leftward, usually producing an upright P wave in lead I and a negative P wave in aVR.
expl: Although lead I is correctly upright, aVR normally records a negative P wave.
This reverses the expected normal limb-lead polarity.
Although aVR is correctly negative, the P wave in lead I normally points upward.

items.subject: Physiology
items.stem: An endurance athlete has a resting heart rate of 50/min. Each QRS complex is preceded by a normal sinus P wave with a constant PR interval. Which structure is initiating the rhythm?
items.rationale: Normal sinus P waves establish that atrial activation begins in the SA node; a slow rate alone does not imply an escape pacemaker.
expl: An AV-junctional escape rhythm does not ordinarily produce the stated normal sinus activation sequence.
The His bundle conducts impulses to the ventricles but is not the initiating site in sinus rhythm.
A ventricular escape pacemaker would not explain normal sinus P waves consistently initiating conducted beats.

items.subject: Physiology
items.stem: Verapamil blocks L-type calcium channels in nodal cells. Which direct change in their action potential is expected?
items.rationale: The nodal phase 0 upstroke depends on calcium entry. L-type calcium-channel blockade slows this calcium-dependent depolarization.
expl: A steeper pacemaker slope would accelerate automaticity rather than describe the direct blocked calcium upstroke.
Fast sodium channels do not generate the nodal phase 0 upstroke.
Blocking the inward calcium current slows rather than accelerates the upstroke.

items.stem: Aortic valve closure contributes to the second heart sound. Which left ventricular phase begins immediately afterward?
items.rationale: After the aortic valve closes and before the mitral valve opens, the ventricle relaxes at constant volume.
expl: Isovolumetric contraction follows mitral closure and precedes aortic opening.
Rapid filling begins after the mitral valve opens, following isovolumetric relaxation.
Ejection occurs while the aortic valve is open.

items.rationale: Sympathetic stimulation increases the probability that If channels are open, accelerating diastolic depolarization and pacemaker firing.
expl: Acetylcholine-mediated potassium effects favor slowing rather than the sympathetic response.

Sodium entry through fast sodium channels

expl: Ligand-gated chloride influx is not the principal inward plateau current.

Fast sodium influx produces phase 0 rather than maintaining the plateau.

items.subject: Physiology
items.stem: On an ECG recorded at 25 mm/s, successive R waves are separated by 10 small squares. Which pairing gives the calculated heart rate and expected diastolic filling time compared with 75/min?
items.rationale: Ten small squares represent 0.4 seconds, corresponding to 150/min. Tachycardia shortens diastole and reduces the time available for filling.
expl: The rate is correct, but faster heart rates shorten rather than lengthen diastole.
The filling-time direction is correct, but ten small squares equal 0.4 seconds, giving 150/min.
Ten small squares give 150/min, and diastole becomes shorter rather than longer.

items.subject: Physiology
items.stem: During quiet tidal expiration in a healthy person, which muscular change permits passive lung recoil?
options: Contraction of the diaphragm and external intercostals
Relaxation of the diaphragm and external intercostals
Contraction of the diaphragm with abdominal relaxation
Contraction of the sternocleidomastoids with inspiratory expansion
items.rationale: Quiet expiration follows relaxation of the inspiratory muscles; elastic recoil reduces lung volume and drives air outward.
expl: These inspiratory contractions expand the chest instead of allowing passive recoil.
Diaphragmatic contraction favors inspiration rather than quiet expiration.
The sternocleidomastoids are accessory inspiratory muscles and do not produce passive expiration.

items.subject: Physiology
items.stem: A person rescued from a house fire has carbon monoxide bound to hemoglobin. How does this affect oxygen binding at the remaining available heme sites?
options: Unchanged affinity, with normal tissue unloading
Lower affinity, shifting the dissociation curve rightward
Absent cooperativity, producing a linear binding curve
Higher affinity, shifting the dissociation curve leftward
items.rationale: Carbon monoxide increases oxygen affinity at the remaining sites, shifting the curve leftward and impairing tissue unloading while also reducing oxygen-carrying capacity.
expl: Affinity and unloading are altered even though arterial dissolved oxygen may remain normal.
A right shift would facilitate unloading, opposite to the carbon monoxide effect.
The characteristic change is increased affinity and reduced capacity, not a linear oxygen-binding curve.

items.subject: Physiology
items.stem: A child aspirates a foreign body that obstructs a segmental bronchus. Alveolar oxygen tension falls distal to the obstruction. What local vascular response redirects blood away from that segment?
items.rationale: Low alveolar oxygen triggers local pulmonary arteriolar constriction, reducing perfusion of poorly ventilated lung.
expl: Bronchial venular dilation is not the pulmonary vascular matching response.
Pulmonary venous constriction is not the principal mechanism of hypoxic pulmonary vasoconstriction.
Dilation would increase perfusion of an inadequately ventilated segment.

items.subject: Physiology
items.stem: In a healthy awake adult, arterial carbon dioxide rises acutely from 40 to 50 mm Hg. Which response is expected from intact central respiratory control?
options: Increased ventilation after brain-fluid hydrogen ions rise
Reduced ventilation after brain-fluid hydrogen ions rise
Reduced ventilation after brain-fluid hydrogen ions fall
Increased ventilation after brain-fluid hydrogen ions fall
items.rationale: CO2 enters brain extracellular fluid and increases hydrogen-ion concentration. Central chemoreceptor stimulation increases the rate and depth of breathing.
expl: Increased brain hydrogen ions stimulate rather than suppress ventilation.
A reduction in hydrogen ions and ventilation describes the opposite CO2 perturbation.
The CO2 rise lowers brain-fluid pH rather than lowering hydrogen-ion concentration.

items.subject: Physiology
items.stem: A patient has persistent respiratory acidosis from chronic hypoventilation. Which delayed renal response helps compensate?
options: Increased bicarbonate reabsorption with reduced acid excretion
Increased bicarbonate reabsorption and net acid excretion
Reduced bicarbonate reabsorption with reduced acid excretion
Reduced bicarbonate reabsorption with increased acid excretion
items.rationale: Renal compensation raises plasma bicarbonate during sustained respiratory acidosis, helping restore the bicarbonate-to-CO2 ratio.
expl: Bicarbonate conservation increases, but net acid excretion does not decrease as the compensatory response.
Reducing bicarbonate conservation and acid excretion would aggravate the acidosis.
Acid excretion increases, but reducing bicarbonate conservation would oppose compensation.

items.subject: Physiology
items.stem: In classic gastrointestinal physiology terminology, increased colonic motility associated with rising in the morning is called which reflex?
items.rationale: The orthocolic reflex describes increased colonic motility associated with rising in the morning.
expl: The gastroileal reflex involves ileal activity in response to gastric stimulation rather than the named morning colonic response.
The defecation reflex is initiated by rectal distension rather than simply arising in the morning.
The gastrocolic response is associated with eating.

options: Inappropriately reduced lower esophageal sphincter tone
Persistently increased lower esophageal sphincter tone
items.rationale: Transient inappropriate LES relaxation or reduced barrier pressure permits reflux from the stomach into the esophagus.
expl: Pyloric tone controls gastric emptying into the duodenum, not the gastroesophageal barrier itself.
The upper sphincter is not the main barrier between stomach and esophagus.
High LES tone impedes passage into the stomach and is more characteristic of outflow obstruction.

Gallbladder relaxation with sphincter of Oddi relaxation

items.stem: Which pairing correctly distinguishes the roles of bile salts and pancreatic lipase in fat digestion?

Bile salts emulsify fat; lipase emulsifies triglycerides
Bile salts emulsify fat; lipase hydrolyzes triglycerides
Bile salts hydrolyze fat; lipase hydrolyzes triglycerides

expl: This swaps nonenzymatic emulsification with enzymatic hydrolysis.

Lipase hydrolyzes triglycerides, but bile salts disperse droplets rather than cleaving their ester bonds.

Compression of the right optic nerve

A right optic nerve lesion causes right monocular visual loss.

items.stem: During labor, cervical stretching promotes oxytocin release, which strengthens contractions and produces further stretching. What type of control loop is operating?

expl: Negative feedback would oppose rather than amplify the initial stretch.
Tonic inhibition is a sustained restraining influence rather than this escalating stimulus-response loop.
Feedforward anticipates a disturbance rather than amplifying a measured consequence.

items.subject: Physiology
items.stem: What is an important function of reversible binding of a circulating hormone to plasma proteins?
options: Promoting rapid filtration of the intact protein-hormone complex
Delivering the bound complex directly into nuclear receptors
Maintaining a reservoir that replenishes free hormone
Preventing any hormone dissociation into the free fraction
items.rationale: Reversibly bound hormone forms a reservoir. As free hormone leaves the circulation or is metabolized, dissociation can replenish the free fraction.
expl: Binding to a large plasma protein does not promote rapid filtration of the intact complex.
The hormone must dissociate for its free fraction to access receptors; the binding complex is not the nuclear ligand.
Reversibility is essential to a reservoir; irreversible trapping would not replenish free hormone.

items.stem: A patient with end-stage kidney disease and longstanding secondary hyperparathyroidism develops autonomous parathyroid secretion, very high PTH, and persistent hypercalcemia. What is this state called?

PTH resistance usually produces hypocalcemia with high PTH, not this autonomous hypercalcemic state.

items.stem: An adult has a serum creatinine concentration within the laboratory reference interval. Which conclusion about glomerular filtration is most appropriate?

The value alone cannot establish a normal GFR
The value is unaffected by skeletal muscle mass
The value excludes mild loss of kidney function

Muscle mass affects creatinine production and therefore its interpretation.
Mild or moderate kidney injury may not be detected reliably by creatinine concentration alone.

It becomes stronger because collecting ducts secrete sodium
It remains intact because this segment transports only water

Less salt transport into the interstitium weakens rather than strengthens the gradient.

items.subject: Physiology
items.stem: Plasma glucose is 120 mg/dL, and no glucose is excreted in the urine. What is the renal clearance of glucose?
items.rationale: Clearance equals urine concentration times urine flow divided by plasma concentration. With zero urinary glucose excretion, glucose clearance is zero despite ongoing filtration and reabsorption.
expl: A positive clearance requires glucose excretion, which is absent.
This positive value would require an excreted glucose load.
A value near GFR would imply glucose is excreted rather than completely reabsorbed.

items.subject: Physiology
items.stem: A patient has several days of vomiting with loss of gastric acid. Which arterial blood gas pattern best fits the primary acid-base disturbance with an appropriate respiratory response?
options: pH 7.27, PaCO2 60 mm Hg, bicarbonate 27 mEq/L
pH 7.30, PaCO2 30 mm Hg, bicarbonate 14 mEq/L
pH 7.50, PaCO2 48 mm Hg, bicarbonate 36 mEq/L
pH 7.52, PaCO2 25 mm Hg, bicarbonate 20 mEq/L
items.rationale: Gastric acid loss produces metabolic alkalosis. Elevated bicarbonate raises pH, and compensatory hypoventilation increases PaCO2. The supplied values are internally consistent with the Henderson-Hasselbalch relationship.
expl: This is predominantly respiratory acidosis.
Low bicarbonate and acidemia indicate metabolic acidosis.
Low PaCO2 with alkalemia indicates respiratory alkalosis.

items.stem: An otherwise stable patient has primary metabolic alkalosis. Which respiratory response tends to limit the rise in pH?
options: Increased alveolar ventilation with reduced PaCO2
Reduced alveolar ventilation with increased PaCO2
Increased alveolar ventilation with increased PaCO2
Reduced alveolar ventilation with reduced PaCO2

expl: Hyperventilation would lower CO2 and worsen alkalemia.
Higher alveolar ventilation lowers rather than raises PaCO2.
For a given CO2 production rate, lower alveolar ventilation raises rather than lowers PaCO2.

items.subject: Physiology
items.stem: A woman with a recently missed menstrual period and breast tenderness has a negative urine pregnancy test. Which laboratory test is the most sensitive next test for suspected early pregnancy?
items.rationale: Blood hCG testing can detect small amounts of hCG earlier than routine urine testing. The result establishes hCG presence but does not by itself locate a pregnancy.
expl: Estriol is not the preferred early biochemical pregnancy-detection marker.
Urinary estrogen is not the preferred early biochemical pregnancy-detection marker.
Progesterone may inform assessment in selected settings but does not replace sensitive hCG detection.

items.subject: Physiology
items.stem: In a 47,XXX fetus without a testis-determining signal or anti-Müllerian hormone, the paramesonephric ducts contribute to which structure?
items.rationale: Without Müllerian inhibition, the paramesonephric ducts form female internal structures including the uterus, uterine tubes, and proximal vagina.
expl: The ductus deferens is a mesonephric duct derivative.
Testes develop from gonadal tissue under a testis-determining signal, not from paramesonephric ducts.
The prostate develops from the urogenital sinus.

items.subject: Physiology
items.stem: A man uses high-dose exogenous androgens over several months. Which change in endogenous reproductive function is expected?
options: Reduced gonadotropin signaling and reduced sperm production
Increased gonadotropin signaling and reduced sperm production
Increased gonadotropin signaling and increased sperm production
Reduced gonadotropin signaling and increased sperm production
items.rationale: Exogenous androgens suppress the hypothalamic-pituitary-gonadal axis, reducing intratesticular testosterone and sperm production.
expl: Reduced sperm production is expected, but the feedback effect lowers rather than raises gonadotropin signaling.
Feedback suppresses rather than raises gonadotropin signaling.
Suppression reduces the hormonal support required for spermatogenesis rather than increasing it.

items.stem: A 17-year-old girl has absent breast development, low estradiol, and low LH and FSH. MRI shows a pituitary mass. Deficiency of which pituitary hormone group directly explains the delayed gonadal maturation?
items.rationale: LH and FSH provide pituitary stimulation to the gonads. Their deficiency causes hypogonadotropic hypogonadism and impaired pubertal maturation.
expl: ACTH stimulates adrenal cortisol secretion rather than ovarian follicular maturation.
ADH regulates renal water handling rather than pubertal gonadal maturation.
GH deficiency impairs growth but does not directly replace the missing gonadotropic stimulation specified here.

Extracellular volume increases; intracellular volume increases
Extracellular volume decreases; intracellular volume is unchanged

An infused extracellular load does not initially decrease extracellular volume.

items.stem: A patient with low ionized calcium has muscle cramps and facial twitching when the facial nerve is tapped. Which electrophysiological change contributes to the increased excitability?
options: A higher threshold for action-potential initiation
A prolonged inability to open sodium channels
A lower threshold for action-potential initiation

expl: A higher threshold would make the membrane less excitable.
Preventing sodium-channel opening would reduce rather than increase firing.
Greater inhibitory chloride conductance would oppose the observed excitation.

By mechanically altering the coupled ryanodine receptor
By cleaving calcium from troponin C
By pumping calcium directly into the cytoplasm

expl: Myosin ATP hydrolysis drives cross-bridge cycling after calcium release.

The DHPR does not act as a calcium pump.

items.stem: A skeletal-muscle sarcomere is stretched beyond its optimal length so that actin-myosin overlap decreases. What happens to active force generation?
options: Active force decreases as available cross-bridges decrease
Active force increases as available cross-bridges decrease
Active force decreases as available cross-bridges increase
Active force increases as available cross-bridges increase
items.rationale: Beyond optimal overlap, fewer actin sites are accessible to myosin heads, reducing active tension. Passive tension is a separate property and may rise with stretch.
expl: Available cross-bridges decrease, which lowers rather than raises active force.
Active force decreases, but overstretch reduces rather than increases available cross-bridges.
Reduced filament overlap lowers rather than raises the number of available cross-bridges and active force.

items.subject: Physiology
items.stem: At the start of one brief, forceful biceps curl, which energy sources provide the most immediate ATP support?
options: Oxidative ATP production from amino acids
Oxidative ATP production from fatty acids
items.rationale: Preexisting ATP supports the first moments of contraction, and phosphocreatine rapidly regenerates ATP during the first seconds of intense activity.

Fat oxidation supplies energy during sustained activity, but is not the most immediate ATP buffer at contraction onset.
Glycolysis contributes to intense activity, but stored ATP and phosphocreatine provide the earliest immediate support.

items.subject: Physiology
items.stem: As voluntary force demand rises from low to maximal in a skeletal muscle, which recruitment pattern is expected?
options: Only large units during every voluntary contraction
Small units first, followed by additional larger units
Only small units throughout the full force range
Large units first, with small units progressively silenced
items.rationale: Low-threshold small motor units are recruited first. Greater force demand recruits progressively larger units; maximal recruitment involves the available small and large units.
expl: Large units are not the sole units used for low-force voluntary tasks.
Small units alone do not provide the full force reserve of the muscle.
This reverses the usual size-dependent recruitment sequence.

Right shift with increased oxygen unloading

Left shift with unchanged oxygen unloading

Increased potassium uptake directly into the sarcoplasmic reticulum

expl: Potassium uptake into the SR is not the mechanism linking pump inhibition to stronger contraction.
The positive inotropic effect results from increased rather than reduced calcium availability.
Greater calcium extrusion would reduce contractile calcium.

End-systolic volume decreases and stroke volume increases

items.stem: A normal lung approaches total lung capacity. A large additional transpulmonary pressure produces only a small volume increase. What does this indicate?
options: High compliance at that high lung volume
Low compliance at that high lung volume
Low elastic recoil at that high lung volume
High compliance because pressure change is large

expl: High compliance would produce a larger volume change for the pressure increment.

The ratio is small when pressure changes greatly but volume changes little.

items.stem: Which lipid-digestion product can enter villus capillary blood and reach the liver through the portal vein without first being packaged into a chylomicron?

Long-chain fatty acids are re-esterified and packaged for chylomicron transport through lacteals.

expl: Potassium conductance occurs through potassium channels, not CFTR.
Sodium is a cation and is not the anion conducted by CFTR.

items.subject: Physiology
items.stem: PTH promotes an increase in circulating calcium. Which hormone can oppose this direction by inhibiting osteoclastic bone resorption?
items.rationale: Calcitonin inhibits bone resorption and can lower circulating calcium. Its role in routine adult calcium homeostasis is limited, so this does not imply that it is an equally important reciprocal regulator of PTH.
expl: ADH regulates water handling and osmolality rather than directly inhibiting osteoclastic bone resorption.
GH supports growth largely through IGF-1 rather than serving as the named calcitonin-like antiresorptive signal.
Glucagon primarily regulates fuel availability, especially blood glucose.

Deiodination removes iodine rather than joining two iodotyrosyl residues.
Endocytosis takes iodinated thyroglobulin into the follicular cell for processing.

items.stem: A child has untreated primary congenital hypothyroidism from an intrinsic thyroid defect. Which laboratory pattern is expected?
options: High free T4 with high TSH
High free T4 with low TSH
Low free T4 with low TSH
Low free T4 with high TSH

expl: High T4 does not fit untreated failure of thyroid hormone synthesis in this case.
High T4 with suppressed TSH is typical of primary thyroid hormone excess.
Low T4 with inadequate TSH suggests a central hypothalamic or pituitary disorder.

items.stem: A 13-year-old with new-onset type 1 diabetes presents with dehydration, deep breathing, glucose of 600 mg/dL, and pH of 7.15. Which cellular change is expected from insulin deficiency?
options: Increased glucose uptake through adipocyte GLUT4
Increased synthesis of skeletal muscle protein
items.rationale: Insulin normally promotes GLUT4-mediated glucose uptake in adipose tissue and muscle. Its deficiency reduces this uptake while favoring catabolic fuel mobilization.
expl: Insulin restrains lipolysis; deficiency permits increased triglyceride breakdown.
Insulin deficiency reduces insulin-stimulated GLUT4 glucose uptake rather than increasing it.
Insulin is anabolic for protein; deficiency does not increase its muscle protein-synthesis effect.

options: Gut hormones reduce beta-cell responsiveness to glucose
Gut hormones reduce glucose entry into beta cells
Gut incretins enhance beta-cell responsiveness to glucose
Gut hormones accelerate hepatic insulin clearance

expl: Reduced beta-cell responsiveness would diminish rather than enhance insulin secretion.
Reducing glucose stimulation would not explain the greater insulin response.

items.stem: As glucose metabolism raises the ATP-to-ADP ratio in a pancreatic beta cell, which event initiates membrane depolarization?
options: Opening of chloride channels to hyperpolarize the cell
items.rationale: Higher ATP closes ATP-sensitive K+ channels, reducing potassium efflux. Depolarization then opens voltage-gated calcium channels and triggers insulin exocytosis.
expl: The proposed hyperpolarizing chloride conductance would oppose the stated depolarization.
Calcium-channel opening follows depolarization; closing them reduces the secretory calcium signal.
Opening these K+ channels favors potassium efflux and opposes depolarization.

items.stem: An aldosterone-secreting adrenal adenoma causes resistant hypertension. Which electrolyte and acid-base pattern can result?
items.rationale: Aldosterone increases distal sodium reabsorption, potassium secretion, and hydrogen-ion secretion. These actions can produce hypokalemia and metabolic alkalosis with increased bicarbonate. Normal potassium does not exclude primary aldosteronism.
expl: This reverses the usual potassium and bicarbonate effects of aldosterone excess.
Aldosterone promotes potassium secretion, so high potassium is the wrong direction.
Potassium loss fits, but enhanced hydrogen secretion favors metabolic alkalosis and higher bicarbonate.

expl: Efferent dilation lowers glomerular capillary pressure and is not the principal afferent action of these prostaglandins.
Afferent constriction reduces inflow and opposes this protective effect.
Efferent constriction is associated with angiotensin II rather than the principal protective prostaglandin action.

items.subject: Physiology
items.stem: How does glucose cross the apical membrane from tubular fluid into an early proximal tubular cell?
options: Primary active glucose transport by an ATPase
items.rationale: Apical sodium-glucose cotransport couples glucose entry to the sodium gradient. Basolateral glucose exit uses a different transport mechanism.
expl: Sodium and glucose enter together through a cotransporter; they are not exchanged in opposite directions.
SGLT uses the sodium gradient indirectly; it is not an ATPase pumping glucose alone.
Facilitated glucose diffusion describes basolateral exit rather than the specified apical uptake.

items.subject: Physiology
items.stem: Urine creatinine is 100 mg/dL, plasma creatinine is 1 mg/dL, and urine flow is 1 mL/min. What is the creatinine clearance?
items.rationale: Clearance equals urine concentration times urine flow divided by plasma concentration: (100 mg/dL × 1 mL/min)/(1 mg/dL) = 100 mL/min.
expl: A clearance of 25 mL/min would require a urine-to-plasma ratio or flow one-fourth of the stated product.
50 mL/min is half the value obtained from the supplied concentrations and flow.
200 mL/min doubles the stated concentration-flow product.

items.subject: Physiology
items.stem: In a healthy person with elevated ADH, which nephron segment still reabsorbs the largest fraction of the filtered water load?
items.rationale: The proximal tubule reabsorbs the largest fraction of filtered water, accompanying bulk solute reabsorption. ADH controls final water recovery in the collecting system without making it the largest bulk-reabsorbing segment.
expl: ADH increases collecting-duct water permeability, but most filtered water was already reclaimed upstream.
The descending limb reabsorbs water, but the proximal tubule accounts for the larger filtered fraction.
The early distal convoluted tubule is relatively water-impermeable.

expl: Reduced urea recycling would weaken the medullary osmotic contribution.
The established ADH-dependent process is medullary urea reabsorption, not cortical urea secretion.
Reduced proximal water recovery does not describe the ADH-dependent medullary urea mechanism.

items.subject: Physiology
items.stem: An idealized sodium chloride load is absorbed without water. Before renal excretion, extracellular osmolality rises. What is the initial osmotic response of body cells?
options: Water enters cells and cell volume increases
Water enters cells and cell volume decreases
Water leaves cells and cell volume decreases
Water leaves cells and cell volume increases
items.rationale: The hypertonic extracellular fluid draws water out of cells, reducing intracellular volume until osmotic equilibrium is approached.
expl: Water moves toward the higher extracellular solute concentration, not into cells.
Entry of water would increase rather than decrease cell volume, and the proposed direction is wrong.
Loss of intracellular water decreases rather than increases cell volume.

items.subject: Physiology
items.stem: A large insulin dose can reduce serum potassium through which immediate mechanism?
options: Increased movement of potassium out of cells
Increased movement of potassium into cells
items.rationale: Insulin promotes cellular potassium uptake, shifting potassium out of extracellular fluid. This redistribution can lower serum potassium without initially changing total-body potassium.
expl: Reduced intestinal uptake does not explain the rapid insulin-induced redistribution of circulating potassium.
The immediate insulin effect is cellular uptake rather than a direct increase in potassium filtration.
An outward shift raises extracellular potassium.

expl: Normal-gap acidosis is more typical of bicarbonate loss or selected tubular disorders.
Ketoacid accumulation lowers rather than raises bicarbonate as the primary process.
A primary fall in PaCO2 does not explain accumulation of ketoacids.

expl: Elevated PaCO2 alone is acidifying and does not explain the alkalemia as a primary process.
The pH and bicarbonate are increased rather than decreased.
Primary respiratory alkalosis requires reduced PaCO2, which is absent.

Vibration is associated with specialized mechanoreceptor input rather than free-ending thermoreception.
Joint position relies on proprioceptive receptors rather than cutaneous temperature endings.

items.subject: Physiology
items.stem: During voluntary shortening of a skeletal muscle, what is the purpose of simultaneous gamma-motor-neuron activity?
options: Maintaining spindle sensitivity as the muscle shortens
Replacing Ia sensory input with efferent signals
Directly generating force in extrafusal fibers
Reducing spindle tension to silence Ia afferents
items.rationale: Gamma neurons contract the polar regions of intrafusal fibers. This maintains tension on the sensory region so the spindle can continue signaling during muscle shortening.
expl: Gamma activity adjusts the receptor mechanically; it does not substitute motor signals for the Ia sensory pathway.
Alpha motor neurons directly activate the force-producing extrafusal fibers.
Gamma coactivation prevents excessive unloading rather than deliberately silencing the spindle.

Release of calcium from muscle sarcoplasmic reticulum

Renal anemia is chiefly a production problem related to inadequate erythropoietin.

Monocytes give rise to tissue macrophages and are not the granulocyte defined by this helminthotoxic protein.
Basophil granules are characteristically associated with histamine and heparin, not major basic protein as their defining helminth defense.

items.subject: Physiology
items.stem: A patient with quantitative von Willebrand factor deficiency also has reduced factor VIII activity. Which screening pattern is compatible with this disorder?
options: Low platelet count, normal PT, normal aPTT
Low platelet count, prolonged PT, prolonged aPTT
Normal platelet count, normal PT, prolonged aPTT
Normal platelet count, prolonged PT, normal aPTT
items.rationale: vWF deficiency impairs platelet adhesion and can reduce factor VIII stability. Platelet count and PT are usually normal; aPTT can be prolonged when factor VIII is sufficiently reduced. A normal aPTT does not exclude vWF deficiency.
expl: An isolated low platelet count suggests a thrombocytopenic problem rather than the stated quantitative vWF defect.
Combined thrombocytopenia and prolonged PT/aPTT suggest a broader consumptive or coagulation disorder.
Isolated PT prolongation does not reflect the factor VIII-linked intrinsic-pathway effect.

items.stem: A focal lesion produces loss of the right visual half-field in each eye. Which listed location can account for the defect?
items.rationale: The left optic tract carries information from the right visual field of each eye. Its injury can cause right homonymous hemianopia.

A central chiasmal lesion characteristically affects crossing nasal retinal fibers, producing bitemporal loss.
A left optic-nerve lesion affects vision from the left eye rather than the right half-field in each eye.

items.subject: Physiology
items.stem: After standardized bright-light preadaptation, a typical biphasic dark-adaptation curve is measured with a peripheral test stimulus. Which sequence is expected?
options: An early rod phase followed by a less sensitive cone phase
An early cone phase followed by a more sensitive rod phase
An early rod phase followed by a more sensitive cone phase
An early cone phase followed by a less sensitive rod phase
items.rationale: The early part of a typical biphasic dark-adaptation curve reflects cone recovery. Rod sensitivity later improves enough to detect dimmer stimuli. The curve depends on stimulus and preadaptation conditions.
expl: The first branch is cone-mediated rather than rod-mediated.
The order is reversed: the cone branch precedes the rod-dominated branch.
The later rod phase reaches greater rather than lower sensitivity to dim stimuli under these conditions.

Left sensorineural loss tends to lateralize Weber to the right while preserving AC > BC.

expl: A posterior canal crista also senses angular movement rather than the elevator linear acceleration.
The utricular macula is principally aligned with horizontal linear acceleration.

Legionella stains poorly and requires specialized culture conditions; it is not a typical lactose fermenter.

expl: Mycoplasma lacks a cell wall and is not visible as gram-positive diplococci.
Klebsiella is a gram-negative bacillus, despite also causing lobar pneumonia.
S. aureus forms gram-positive cocci in clusters.

S. mutans is a viridans streptococcus, typically arranged in chains.

Elastin is structural connective tissue rather than the main vegetation scaffold.

Being bitten by an infected mosquito
Ingesting embryonated eggs on contaminated food
Having skin penetrated by infective larvae

Skin penetration is characteristic of hookworm and Strongyloides infection.

Sustained fever, abdominal symptoms, and occasional truncal rose spots

Profuse afebrile watery diarrhea with marked dehydration

options: To treat possible Chlamydia trachomatis coinfection
To treat possible genital herpes coinfection
To provide routine syphilis treatment regardless of testing
To treat possible Trichomonas vaginalis coinfection
items.rationale: Doxycycline provides chlamydia coverage when coinfection has not been excluded. Ceftriaxone treats gonorrhea; doxycycline is administered orally in this regimen.

Trichomoniasis is treated with a nitroimidazole, not doxycycline.

expl: Placenta previa concerns placental location in the uterus rather than tubal transport.
Neural-tube defects are not the characteristic consequence of tubal scarring.
A hydatidiform mole results from abnormal fertilization and trophoblastic development.

items.stem: A teenager develops pruritic, scaly patches of scalp alopecia. Broken hairs contain fungal hyphae. Which fungal genus is the best fit?

Candida commonly causes mucosal disease or intertriginous candidiasis rather than tinea capitis.
Malassezia commonly causes pityriasis versicolor rather than hair-shaft dermatophytosis.

items.subject: Microbiology-Parasitology
items.stem: A nonpregnant, immunocompetent adult with controlled diabetes and hypertension has no evidence of varicella immunity. Household exposure occurred two days ago, and there is no vaccine contraindication. Which intervention is recommended?
items.rationale: Susceptible, vaccine-eligible people should receive varicella vaccine within three to five days after exposure. Diabetes and hypertension alone do not establish an indication for varicella-zoster immune globulin.
expl: Intravenous acyclovir treats severe disease or selected immunocompromised patients; it is not routine prophylaxis for this eligible contact.
Recombinant zoster vaccine prevents shingles and does not replace varicella vaccination for primary-infection prevention.
Immune globulin is used for susceptible exposed people at high risk who cannot receive varicella vaccine.

items.stem: Which immunologic change most directly explains the broad susceptibility to opportunistic infections in advanced untreated HIV infection?
options: Depletion and dysfunction of CD4-positive T cells
Absence of the terminal complement complex
items.rationale: HIV targets CD4-positive cells. Progressive loss of helper T-cell function impairs coordinated cellular immunity and permits opportunistic infections.
expl: Neutropenia may occur but is not the defining immune defect of advanced HIV.
Isolated IgA deficiency does not explain the profound cellular immunodeficiency of AIDS.
Terminal complement deficiency particularly predisposes to Neisseria infection rather than the broad AIDS pattern.

items.stem: A nonventilated adult has no pneumonia at admission. Three days later, a new infiltrate develops with fever, leukocytosis, and purulent sputum. The infection was not incubating at admission. How is this pneumonia classified?
items.rationale: Hospital-acquired pneumonia develops at least 48 hours after admission and was not incubating at admission. A new infiltrate with compatible infection findings supports pneumonia; sputum color alone does not establish it.
expl: Aspiration pneumonitis is a chemical injury rather than this described hospital-acquired infection.
Ventilator-associated pneumonia requires the relevant mechanical-ventilation exposure, which is absent.
Community-acquired pneumonia begins outside the hospital or is present or incubating at admission.

items.stem: A patient with bacterial pneumonia develops infection-associated systemic vasodilation, persistent hypotension despite initial fluid resuscitation, and organ hypoperfusion. Which complication best explains this deterioration?
items.rationale: Septic shock produces a systemic circulatory failure in severe infection. Inflammatory mediators cause vasodilation and impaired perfusion, beyond the local pulmonary injury.
expl: Atelectasis is loss of aerated lung volume rather than systemic infection-associated shock.
A lung abscess is localized suppurative necrosis; it can lead to sepsis but is not the stated circulatory complication.
A parapneumonic effusion is fluid adjacent to the lung and does not itself describe systemic distributive circulatory failure.

Start empiric therapy immediately, ideally within one hour
Withhold therapy until the procalcitonin result returns

expl: A routine 24-hour delay is inappropriate in probable sepsis.
Final culture identification is too slow to guide initiation in probable sepsis.
A biomarker result should not delay indicated treatment in this setting.

items.stem: A critically ill, nonneutropenic adult has newly confirmed candidemia, with susceptibility results pending. Which is the preferred initial drug among these options?
items.rationale: An echinocandin such as micafungin is preferred initial therapy for most adults with candidemia, especially critical illness. Susceptibility results and clinical stability guide later step-down therapy.

Terbinafine treats dermatophyte disease and is not initial therapy for candidemia.
Griseofulvin treats dermatophyte infection, not candidemia.

expl: RNA polymerase synthesizes RNA from a DNA template.

items.subject: Microbiology-Parasitology
items.stem: A child with toxigenic Corynebacterium diphtheriae infection develops a pharyngeal pseudomembrane and myocarditis. Which bacterial factor drives these systemic effects?
options: An endotoxin that activates Toll-like receptor 4
A secreted exotoxin that inhibits protein synthesis
A urease that alkalinizes the mucosa
A capsule that blocks complement assembly
items.rationale: Diphtheria toxin inhibits host protein synthesis through ADP-ribosylation of elongation factor 2. Disseminated toxin can injure the myocardium and nervous system.
expl: Lipopolysaccharide endotoxin is characteristic of gram-negative bacteria, not C. diphtheriae.
Urease activity is not the mechanism of diphtheritic myocarditis.
A capsule does not explain the toxin-mediated systemic injury.

expl: Listeria is a gram-positive rod with a bacterial cell wall.
Listeria has a clinically important intracellular phase.
Obligate intracellular organisms require host cells for replication; Listeria can also grow extracellularly.

expl: C. botulinum produces a neurotoxin causing flaccid paralysis.
B. fragilis is a gram-negative anaerobe associated with intra-abdominal abscesses.
C. tetani produces a neurotoxin causing spastic paralysis.

items.rationale: Acinetobacter is a gram-negative coccobacillus associated with healthcare infections. The oxidase-negative, nonfermenting phenotype distinguishes it from the listed alternatives.
expl: K. pneumoniae is a lactose-fermenting bacillus.
E. coli is a lactose-fermenting enteric bacillus.
P. aeruginosa is usually oxidase positive.

items.rationale: V. cholerae causes marked secretory diarrhea through toxin-mediated cyclic AMP signaling. Rice-water stools and severe fluid loss distinguish this pattern from inflammatory dysentery.
expl: C. jejuni typically causes inflammatory diarrhea, often bloody, rather than profuse rice-water stool.
S. Typhi causes systemic enteric fever rather than this characteristic secretory syndrome.
Shigella causes invasive inflammatory colitis and dysentery.

items.stem: A patient develops abrupt fever and a very painful enlarged regional lymph node after exposure to flea-infested rodents. Which pathogen is most likely?

F. tularensis causes ulceroglandular disease associated with ticks or animal handling.

items.subject: Microbiology-Parasitology
items.stem: An adult has months of cough, weight loss, night sweats, and upper-lobe cavitary disease. Sputum contains acid-fast bacilli. Which organism is the leading diagnosis in this classic presentation?
items.rationale: M. tuberculosis classically produces chronic constitutional symptoms and apical cavitary disease. Acid-fast staining supports mycobacterial infection, with molecular and culture testing needed for definitive identification.
expl: M. leprae primarily affects skin and peripheral nerves.
M. marinum is associated mainly with cutaneous infection after aquatic exposure.
M. scrofulaceum is associated particularly with cervical lymphadenitis in children.

items.stem: A patient with advanced HIV and a CD4 count of 30 cells/mm³ has prolonged fever, weight loss, and diarrhea. Blood cultures grow Mycobacterium avium complex. Which disease pattern is characteristic?
options: Peripheral-nerve and skin infection of leprosy
items.rationale: MAC can cause disseminated disease in profound cellular immunodeficiency, especially with CD4 counts below 50 cells/mm³. Constitutional symptoms and bloodstream involvement support dissemination.
expl: Water-associated localized skin disease suggests M. marinum.
Isolated cervical lymphadenitis is a different, usually localized presentation.
Leprosy is caused by M. leprae and has a different tissue pattern.

S. aureus forms cocci in clusters rather than branching filaments.
Nocardia is aerobic and weakly acid fast.

items.stem: An adult develops pneumonia with diarrhea and hyponatremia after exposure to a contaminated building water system. The organism requires specialized media containing iron and cysteine. Which pathogen fits?
items.rationale: Legionella is acquired from aerosolized water and causes pneumonia with possible gastrointestinal and neurologic findings. Its specialized culture requirements distinguish it from the alternatives.
expl: Mycoplasma causes atypical pneumonia but is not linked to this water-system and culture pattern.
Pneumococcus causes lobar pneumonia but does not require the specified specialized medium.
Klebsiella is a lactose-fermenting encapsulated rod without these culture requirements.

expl: CMV can cause a mononucleosis-like illness but is typically heterophile negative.

HHV-6 classically causes roseola in young children.

Dengue is a positive-sense RNA flavivirus.

Rinsing pork briefly with drinking water
Cooking pork thoroughly before eating it
Removing visible fat before serving it raw

ATP production through viral membrane respiration
Dependence on host-cell machinery for replication
Translation by the virus’s own ribosomes

Viruses do not possess their own complete ribosomal translation machinery.

items.stem: An asymptomatic tourist swallowed water later found to contain Naegleria fowleri, with no water entering the nose. Which explanation is appropriate?
options: Swallowing alone does not transmit this amebic brain infection
Any swallowed exposure requires empiric intravenous treatment
An immediate stool test determines the risk of brain infection
Person-to-person isolation is required after the exposure
items.rationale: N. fowleri infection occurs when contaminated water enters the nose and the amoeba reaches the brain. Swallowing water alone is not the route of this infection. This does not establish that the water is safe from other pathogens.
expl: Antimicrobial treatment is not indicated solely for this isolated ingestion exposure.
Stool testing is not a screening method for future Naegleria brain infection.
Naegleria infection is not transmitted from person to person.

items.stem: Which molecular system powers gliding motility in invasive stages of apicomplexan parasites such as Cryptosporidium and Toxoplasma?
options: Actin filaments interacting with myosin motors
Flagellar rotation driven by a proton gradient
items.rationale: Apicomplexan gliding uses actomyosin machinery coupled to surface adhesins. Subpellicular microtubules contribute to cellular architecture but are not the force-generating motor described here.
expl: Axonemal dynein drives ciliary or flagellar bending rather than apicomplexan gliding.
Actin-driven pseudopod extension characterizes amoeboid movement; the gliding mechanism here depends on myosin motors interacting with actin.
Proton-driven rotary flagella are characteristic of bacteria.
